Larval development in African tigerfish (Hydrocynus vittatus) proceeds rapidly under controlled thermal conditions. At a constant water temperature of 28 °C [T = 28 °C], yolk-sac larvae emerge from the chorion after approximately 22.5 hours , a relatively brief incubation period typical of pelagic-spawning characids. Upon eclosion, these prolarvae measure a mere 0.29 cm  in total length, possessing a prominent yolk sac that sustains them during the non-feeding stage. Within a few days, the yolk reserves are largely absorbed, and by an age of 5.4375 days [ab = 5.4375 days] since fertilisation, corresponding to roughly 4.5 days after hatching, the first exogenous feeding begins as the mouth opens and retinal differentiation allows prey detection at a temperature of 28 °C [T = 28 °C]. At the onset of exogenous feeding, the total length of the larvae is approximately 0.45 cm [Lb = approximately 0.45 cm]. By 13 days post-hatch, individuals have grown substantially, reaching a total length of 0.8 cm , a size at which they become increasingly efficient planktonic predators in the water column at a temperature of 28 °C [T = 28 °C].

Growth continues at a steady pace during the subsequent larval and early juvenile phases. At a rearing temperature of 28 °C [T = 28 °C], 40-day-old tigerfish attain an average total length of 4 cm , reflecting a period of muscular development and fin ray ossification. The onset of metamorphosis, involving a reorganisation of the body plan and the transition from a pelagic to a more benthic-oriented lifestyle, occurs at an age of approximately 17.9375 days  since fertilisation, corresponding to roughly 17 days after hatching, when individuals typically measure about 1 cm  in total length at a temperature of 28 °C [T = 28 °C]. These post-metamorphic juveniles begin to exhibit the predatory morphology characteristic of the genus, including sharper dentition and a more streamlined form. By 72 days post-hatch under the same thermal regime, the fingerlings have reached a total length of 5 cm , a size at which they are capable of consuming relatively large prey items and are less vulnerable to gape-limited predators.

Sexual maturation in Hydrocynus vittatus is associated with a considerable size threshold. Data from field surveys indicate that puberty is attained at a total length of approximately 39.8 cm [Lp = approximately 39.8 cm], a size that corresponds to a robust, actively foraging sub-adult. The age at which this reproductive activation occurs has been estimated from length-at-age relationships; under the standard thermal conditions of 28 °C [T = 28 °C], the first spawning event is thought to occur at around 975 days [tR = around 975 days] after hatching. This timing is relatively protracted compared to smaller characid species, likely reflecting the energetic demands of achieving a large body size before gonadal development can be completed. Vitellogenesis and spermiation onset are presumably cued by a combination of photoperiod and temperature in the floodplain rivers this species inhabits, with the onset of the rainy season triggering synchronised breeding aggregations.

The reproductive capacity of mature African tigerfish is considerable. Spawning females achieve a daily egg production rate that, when expressed in more natural terms, equates to roughly 937 eggs per day. This annual reproductive output is achieved through a pattern of intermittent spawning events; females produce approximately 70,000 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 70,000 eggs per spawning event], and may spawn approximately 5 times per breeding season [F_R_i = approximately 5 times per breeding season]. This high investment in fecundity is typical of large-bodied freshwater predators that experience unpredictable recruitment conditions and high larval mortality in floodplain environments. The maximum adult wet weight recorded for this species is 28,000 grams [Wwi = 28,000 grams], a limit that is reached only by the oldest and most dominant individuals in a population. Correspondingly, the ultimate total length approaches 105 cm [Li = 105 cm], a size that places Hydrocynus vittatus among the largest freshwater characins.

Longevity in African tigerfish is moderate for a fish of its maximum size. Field records and otolith-based age estimates indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 8 years [am = approximately 8 years] under natural conditions, when maintained at the species' optimal thermal range of 28 °C [T = 28 °C]. Individuals achieving this age have typically attained the ultimate body mass of 28 kilograms [Wwi = 28 kilograms], a metric that underscores the substantial tissue investment required for post-pubertal growth. The relatively short generation time, combined with high fecundity and a large asymptotic size, positions Hydrocynus vittatus as a resilient predator within its ecosystem, capable of rapid population recovery following disturbance, yet vulnerable to overfishing of the large, reproductively valuable females that represent the greatest spawning potential.
